# Contributing to mycolorsTB

mycolorsTB is a small R package: colour palettes for *Mycobacterium
tuberculosis* complex data, the ggplot2 scales that apply them, and two helpers
that draw a tree with ggtree. Eleven exported objects in one file. Most useful
contributions are small too, such as a palette that fails on a real dataset, a
helper that errors unhelpfully or does not error when it should, or a
documentation line that misled you.

Maintainer: Paula Ruiz-Rodriguez, paula.ruiz.rodriguez@csic.es.

## Reporting a problem

Open an issue at
[github.com/PathoGenOmics-Lab/mycolorsTB/issues](https://github.com/PathoGenOmics-Lab/mycolorsTB/issues).
The forms cover the two common cases and label themselves, so there is nothing
for you to set by hand.

What makes a report actionable is the call and the output, not a description of
either. Paste `packageVersion("mycolorsTB")`, the R version and platform from
`sessionInfo()`, the exact call you made, and what R printed. If a plot came out
wrong, the code that produced it is worth more than a screenshot of it, because
the screenshot cannot be run.

Security problems do not go in the issue tracker. See
[SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md).

## Setting up

Two of the four imports come from CRAN. `grDevices` ships with R itself, and
`ggtree` comes from Bioconductor.

```r
install.packages(c("devtools", "roxygen2", "ggplot2", "ape", "knitr", "rmarkdown"))
if (!requireNamespace("BiocManager", quietly = TRUE)) install.packages("BiocManager")
BiocManager::install("ggtree")
```

`ggtree` is a Bioconductor package, so `install.packages("ggtree")` will not
find it and fails with a "package is not available" message that reads like you
made a typo rather than like you used the wrong repository. If `R CMD check`
tells you `ggtree` is missing, that is what happened. This is a prerequisite,
not an optional extra: `NAMESPACE` has `import(ggtree)`, so the package will not
load without it.

`knitr` and `rmarkdown` are in that list for a similar reason. They are only
`Suggests`, so nothing pulls them in for you, but `DESCRIPTION` sets
`VignetteBuilder: knitr` and `devtools::check()` builds
`vignettes/use-mycolors.Rmd` before it checks anything. Without the vignette
engine the run stops during `R CMD build`, having tested nothing.

## The development loop

Use `devtools::load_all()` while you work. It loads the package from source into
the session, so you can change `R/classicTB.R` and call the function again
without installing anything.

Run `devtools::document()` after **any** change to a roxygen comment, and treat
the files it rewrites as output. `NAMESPACE` says "Generated by roxygen2: do not
edit by hand" in its first line, and every file under `man/` is generated in the
same way. Editing them directly appears to work right up to the next
`document()` run, which silently discards the edit.

The reverse of that has already happened in this repository, and it is the
reason this section exists. `man/plot_tb_tree.Rd` and
`man/plot_tb_cladogram.Rd` shipped `\dontrun{}` while the roxygen comments in
`R/classicTB.R` said `\donttest{}`. The generated files had drifted from their
source, so the next `devtools::document()` would have flipped CRAN from skipping
those examples to running them, inside a commit whose diff looked like routine
documentation. Nobody would have chosen that. It would simply have happened on
the next unrelated change.

So: run `document()` as part of the change rather than afterwards, and read the
diff it produces. If a `.Rd` file changes in a way you did not intend, that is
not noise. It means the comment and the generated file had already disagreed,
and you have just found out when.

## Before opening a pull request

```r
devtools::document()
devtools::check()
```

`R CMD check` is the bar you clear before pushing, and locally it is the whole
bar: this repository has no `tests/` directory yet. That is thinner than it
sounds, because the examples for `plot_tb_tree()` and `plot_tb_cladogram()` are
wrapped in `\dontrun{}`, so `check()` reads them and never runs them. CI then
runs the same check across five platform and R version pairings, plus a second
job that checks the generated documentation; see the next section.

That is one half of the problem. The other half is how rarely the bar was
applied at all, and `view_palette()` is on record for it. The function used the
`size` aesthetic on `geom_tile`, which ggplot2 deprecated in 3.4.0, and the
deprecation warning told every user to report the issue to the authors. The
vignette calls `view_palette()` in a chunk that is evaluated, so `check()`
builds the vignette, runs the function, and would have printed that warning on
any run at all. No check ran automatically at the time, so there was no such run
between the ggplot2 upgrade and the release, and the warning reached users
first. Tests are therefore a welcome contribution in their own right, and
so is any change that lets `check()` execute a function it currently only reads.

Two check notes are worth knowing about in advance. The first has already been
paid for once:

- **Non-standard files at the top level.** `images/` is listed in
  `.Rbuildignore` for this reason. Anything else you add at the top level needs
  the same treatment, or `R CMD check` reports it and the source tarball carries
  it to CRAN. The images alone were around 490 KB of PNGs that the README
  renders from GitHub anyway.
- **Undocumented exports.** Adding an `@export` without running `document()`
  leaves `NAMESPACE` and `man/` behind, and `check()` is where you find out.

## What runs on your pull request

[`.github/workflows/ci.yml`](workflows/ci.yml) runs `R CMD check` on five legs:
Ubuntu with R release, R devel and R oldrel-1, macOS with R release, and Windows
with R release. It fails on a WARNING rather than on a NOTE, so the two notes
above are still yours to read rather than something the run blocks on.

The same workflow has a second job, and it is an independent gate. It installs
roxygen2, regenerates the documentation on a clean checkout, and fails the run
if `man/`, `NAMESPACE` or `DESCRIPTION` differ from what it produced. That is
the drift described further up, caught at the pull request instead of shipped in
a later unrelated commit.

[`codeql.yml`](workflows/codeql.yml) and
[`dependency-review.yml`](workflows/dependency-review.yml) run on every pull
request too. Both look at the workflows rather than at the R code: CodeQL has no
extractor for R, and GitHub's dependency graph does not read a `DESCRIPTION`
file.

None of that replaces running `document()` and `check()` before you push. A red
run tells you what your own machine would have told you, several minutes later
and in front of everyone.

## NEWS.md

A change to behaviour gets a line in `NEWS.md`, under the heading for the
version in development. Behaviour means anything a user can observe: a colour
that changed, an argument that is now validated, a warning that no longer fires,
a call that now errors where it used to return a broken plot. Internal
refactoring does not need an entry.

This is not bookkeeping. `NEWS.md` is what somebody reads when a figure they
made last year comes out different, and it is what a CRAN reviewer reads on
submission. The version heading there and the `Version:` field in `DESCRIPTION`
move together.

## Labels

Do not apply labels by hand. Pull requests are labelled automatically from
[`.github/labeler.yml`](labeler.yml), from the paths they touch: `R/` gets `r`;
`man/`, `vignettes/`, `README.md` and `NEWS.md` get `documentation`;
`DESCRIPTION`, `NAMESPACE` and `.Rbuildignore` get `packaging`; `tests/` gets
`tests`; anything under `.github/` gets `ci`. Issues opened through the forms
carry their own labels, set by the form.

Most real changes here collect several at once, and that is the point rather
than a defect in the rules. Adding an exported function touches `R/`, `man/` and
`NAMESPACE`, so it arrives carrying `r`, `documentation` and `packaging`
together. The case worth a second look is the one where they come apart: a pull
request labelled `r` but not `documentation` usually means `document()` was not
run. That is a hint and not the check. The drift itself is caught by the
documentation job in [`ci.yml`](workflows/ci.yml), which regenerates `man/` and
`NAMESPACE` and turns the run red on any difference, so nobody has to spot it in
the label shape.

If your pull request arrives with no label at all, the rule for that path is
missing from `.github/labeler.yml`. Adding it in the same pull request is a fair
fix.

## Dependabot

The only ecosystem configured is GitHub Actions. An R package has no lockfile to
update, and the package's own dependencies are resolved by CRAN and Bioconductor
at install time, not pinned here.

Routine minor and patch bumps to the actions merge themselves once CI is green,
through [`.github/workflows/dependabot-auto-merge.yml`](workflows/dependabot-auto-merge.yml).
Major bumps never do. They arrive in their own pull request and wait for a
person, because a major version of an action can change or remove its inputs,
and an action that quietly stops doing what it used to is precisely the failure
a green tick hides.

## Branches and pull requests

Work on a branch and open a pull request. This holds for your own changes and it
holds when you have permission to push to `main`: never push straight to `main`.
CI runs on the pull request, but the trigger is not the point. The pull request
is where the reasoning is written down, and in six months the reasoning is the
part you will want back.

One change per pull request. A fix bundled with a refactor is hard to review and
impossible to revert cleanly.

For commit messages, a short subject line and then two or three sentences saying
why. The diff already says what.

Fill in the pull request template. The section that matters is how it was
verified, meaning what you ran and what it printed. For a palette change, name
the palette and give the hex codes before and after. For a helper, give the call
and its output. "Should work" is not verification, and verification is the one
thing a reviewer cannot reconstruct from the diff.
